newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Difficult talks seen on EU gas liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Difficult talks seen on EU gas liberalisation.

text.p: Talks this week have made clear that European Union member states still have widely different views on key aspects of how to liberalise natural gas markets, diplomats said on Tuesday.

"I'm afraid we will have quite substantial problems," one EU diplomat said after Monday's discussions of the Council's energy working group. "You have two camps, which is obvious, the differences are wide."
Britain, the Netherlands and Germany are the most in favour of liberalisation while France and Belgium have adopted a more sceptical attitude.

The diplomat said he was afraid the talks could turn out to be as difficult as the negotiations on opening up EU electricity markets, where a deal was reached only last June after six years of wrangling.
But others said they were still optimistic about the chances of reaching a deal, even as early as during the Dutch presidency next spring.
These diplomats said the deal on electricity would help in smoothing the way for the talks on natural gas, even if there are differences between the two energy sectors.

But they acknowledged that there were different opinions on important issues, such as the level of market freedom and on how to handle long-term "Take or Pay" deals, which dominate the European gas industry.
"I would say there are three or four major problems," one diplomat said.

A further diplomat referred to the negotiations as the usual "ritual dance" adding that while talks in July had shown a high degree of consensus, recent sessions had revealed more divergence in opinions that he had expected.
Monday's talks were the second session to deal with a new compromise proposal from the Irish presidency, put forward earlier this month.
EU diplomats have praised the paper but there are still several question marks and diplomats say member states at this stage naturally tended to advocate "maximalist" positions.
Energy officials have now gone through most of the presidency text and senior energy officials from the 15 capitals, usually ministers, will meet in Brussels next Tuesday.
Monday's session dealt with several potentially controversial aspects of the dossier, explaining the more pessimistic assessment of the situation.
Unlike the agreement on electricity, which foresees a gradual and progressive opening up of national markets, the presidency has proposed a one-off liberalisation for gas.

The proposal uses the same method to calculate the share of the market that would be open to competition as for electricity, including a threshold to determine which consumers will be allowed to shop freely for the best deal.
No figures on the level of market opening have yet been put forward and this looks certain to be a controversial issue.
Germany would like to see EU member states open up their markets completely from the beginning, a position unlikely to go down well with the more cautious.
Reflecting its more interventionist approach, France has put forward the idea of import licences to guarantee the diversification of supplies, one diplomat said.
On "Take or Pay" contracts, those pushing for wide liberalisation believe the Irish proposal goes too far in protecting such deals, while France would like to see much greater protection.
"Take or Pay" contracts may create problems in a liberalised environment as purchasers must buy gas at a set price regardless of whether they have a buyer themselves.

The natural gas dossier will dominate the EU's energy policy work during the final months of the year, even if no one expects an agreement before 1997. Energy ministers will discuss the dossier at their meeting on December 3.
The presidency paper takes the place of the amended Commission proposal COM(93)643, which was put forward in 1993 but left in abeyance while the EU focused on the twin directives on electricity.
Under the deal on electricity nearly a quarter of the EU's market will be open to competition from January 1999 at the earliest. This would rise to about a third by 2003.
It was the result of a compromise, mainly between Germany, which pushed for wide liberalisation, and France, wary of any dramatic opening up of markets.
